archetype.name: Playoff Team (goaltending-first)
archetype.definition: A Boston side that drives play well enough to sit near the top of the Atlantic, with two hot goalies turning a good team into one that looks elite.

report.headline: Better at 5-on-5 than last year, but the goalies are still doing the heavy lifting
report.take:
Boston is 15-7-1, third on the site and third in the league in Goal Diff / GP at 0.96, on pace for 111 points. Last year's 100-point team was built on sand: a 47.3% xGF share propped up by 30.6 goals saved above expected and a 102.3 PDO. This version is a sturdier team. It owns 53.4% of the 5-on-5 expected goals, seventh in the league, so the chance quality is genuinely tilting its way rather than being papered over.

The margin is still inflated. A 5-on-5 PDO of 103.9 and an all-situations save percentage of .910, third in the league against a .891 average, mean the goalies and shooters are both running hot. The 2.65 goals allowed a game, fourth best, sits on top of 27.9 shots against a night, which ranks only 20th. Jeremy Swayman (.905, 6.2 GSAx over 17 starts) has been good. Michael DiPietro (.923, 5.6 GSAx in six starts) has been nearly as valuable in a fraction of the work, and a backup at that level is what tends to come back to earth first. Shot-attempt share is dead even at 50%, so the puck is not living in the other end. Boston gets better looks rather than more of them.

What the numbers hide runs both ways. The record is not padded by close-game luck: Pts vs Goal Diff sits at -1.4, 25th, so if anything Boston has left points on the table relative to its goal differential. The power play is the soft spot. It converts 19.4%, 26th and below the league's 22.5%, after running at 23.4% last year, so some recovery is reasonable to expect. Both of those factors point upward and help offset whatever the save percentage gives back.

The recent stretch is the warning. Over the last five games Boston went 2-3 and allowed 4 goals a game, including three straight home losses to Montreal, Minnesota and LA, and November's goals against rose to 3.13 a game from October's 2.57. That looks like the save percentage starting to normalize toward a shot-against profile that was always middling. Expect a top-10 team that finishes comfortably in the playoffs rather than one that sustains a nearly-a-goal-a-game margin.

strengths.title: Two goalies stealing goals
strengths.body: Boston's goalies are fourth in GSAx at 11.7, and both of them are contributing. Swayman and DiPietro have each saved more than five goals above expected. That depth means a cold week from one does not sink the team, but DiPietro's .923 in a small sample is the part most likely to fade.

strengths.title: Real 5-on-5 chance edge
strengths.body: A 53.4% xGF share, seventh in the league, is a clear step up from last year's 47.3%. That shows the improvement is structural, not just goalie-driven. Hampus Lindholm's 61.7% xGF and +11 in over 20 minutes a night anchor it from the back end.

strengths.title: Wingers shut down completely
strengths.body: Boston has not allowed a goal to an opposing winger. It is first in the league at holding wingers under their expected output, and wingers account for just 14.3% of the points against it versus a 43% league norm. Zero goals is not sustainable, but the coverage on the flanks is clearly a strength.

concerns.title: Percentages running well above normal
concerns.body: A 103.9 PDO and an all-situations 102.1, seventh in the league, combine hot shooting (11.1% against a 9.8% league mark) with elite save percentage. Both tend to drift back toward average. When they do, the gap between a 3rd-ranked goal differential and a 16th-ranked shot-attempt share will narrow.

concerns.title: Defense leaks lately, and from the blue line
concerns.body: Boston has allowed 4 goals a game over the last five, 1.35 above its season rate. Opposing defensemen have produced 52.4% of the points against it, and it ranks 25th at containing them, which points to point shots and pinches getting through. With shots against already middling, this is the area most exposed if the goaltending cools.

concerns.title: Power play below league standard
concerns.body: The power play converts 19.4%, 26th and 3.1 points under the league average, a drop from 23.4% a year ago. Peterka and Minten have just three power-play points between them. Some bounce-back is likely, but right now it is not helping to cover for anything.

trend.note: A dominant October (9-5, 2.57 allowed a game) gave way to a looser November with goals against up to 3.13. That November stretch included a three-game home losing skid before back-to-back wins steadied things.

weekAhead.headline: Three home games against bottom-half teams, including the league's worst
weekAhead.body:
All three games are at home, against teams ranked 21st, 27th and 32nd on the site. This is the softest stretch Boston will see for a while and a chance to stop the goals-against bleeding from the last five. Vancouver is the gift: 32nd in xGF at 39.2%, 32nd in GSAx and killing only 61.2% of penalties. Toronto is a struggling 8-14-3.

The catch is special teams. Winnipeg (23.9%) and Toronto (25.7%) both run top-10 power plays against Boston's middling penalty kill. Winnipeg's shot volume against is the worst in the league, but its 72.5% kill is exactly what a slumping Bruins power play needs to get going. Anything less than two wins would be a disappointment.

keyMatchups.title: Power play vs Vancouver's kill
keyMatchups.body: Vancouver kills 61.2% of penalties, 31st, and Winnipeg is 24th at 72.5%. If Boston's 26th-ranked power play is going to turn, this is the week. Fail to convert here and the problem looks deeper than bad luck.

keyMatchups.title: Peterka against soft winger coverage
keyMatchups.body: Vancouver allows 0.96 points a game to wingers, 31st, and Toronto ranks 24th against them. JJ Peterka, Boston's top-ranked forward at 15 points, should see plenty of room on the right side.

keyMatchups.title: Toronto's power play vs Boston's kill
keyMatchups.body: Toronto converts 25.7%, sixth in the league, while Boston kills a middle-of-the-pack 79.5%. Toronto's -5.2 Pts vs Goal Diff also says it has been unlucky. It is a more dangerous opponent than its record suggests, so discipline matters in that game.

weekAhead.watch: Whether goals against settles back toward the October level against three weak offenses, or keeps running near the 4 a game of the last five.

restOfSeason.body:
The underlying play is good enough to keep Boston in the Atlantic's top three. A 53.4% xGF share and a record that has, if anything, underperformed its goal differential in close games are durable foundations. What will not hold is a .910 save percentage behind a 20th-ranked shot-suppression game, along with shooting nearly a point and a half above league average. Expect goals against to drift up from 2.65 a game toward roughly 2.8 to 3.0, partly offset by a power play that should recover some of last year's form.

That adds up to a team that cools from its 111-point pace but not dramatically. Something near last season's 100 points, or a bit better, is the likely landing spot, with a division title realistic in a tightly bunched top five. The goaltending tandem is the hinge. If Swayman holds up near his current GSAx and DiPietro stays useful, Boston stays near the top. If both regress at once, a mid-pack shot profile leaves it a bubble-adjacent playoff team.
swingFactors: Save percentage regression from both goalies
Power play recovering toward last year's form
Limiting point production from opposing defensemen

confidence.note: 23 games is a modest sample, and the PDO inflation is clear; xGF and history give a firmer read.
